item.title: Riverlane Demonstrates Data-Driven DEM Augmentation to Reduce Surface-Code Logical Errors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it shows a practical way to tighten the gap between theoretical surface‑code performance and what real devices can achieve by letting syndrome data reveal hidden correlated errors. Riverlane’s data‑driven augmentation of Detector Error Models builds on recent machine‑learning‑assisted error‑characterisation efforts, delivering up to a 75 % logical‑error reduction in simulation and a measurable 14 % gain on actual hardware—an encouraging step toward scalable fault tolerance. The results also highlight that while the method scales well in silico, translating those gains fully to noisy quantum processors will require further integration with device‑specific calibration cycles.

Riverlane has developed a data-driven method to improve quantum error correction in surface-code architectures. By identifying unmodeled correlated error mechanisms from syndrome measurement data, their technique augments standard Detector Error Models (DEMs). This approach has shown significant reductions in logical error rates, up to 75% in simulations and 14% on physical hardware. item.description:

By convening banks, quantum vendors and academic groups around a shared synthetic dataset, the FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will generate the first systematic benchmarks that can tell whether QML truly outperforms classical analytics in this domain, echoing similar pilots emerging in fraud detection and cybersecurity worldwide. The initiative also sets an early precedent for policy guidance on data governance and oversight of quantum technologies, though its impact will remain limited until scalable hardware and robust algorithms are demonstrably superior to existing tools.

The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) is launching the Quantum Experimentation Group (QEG) in Q1 2027 to assess if quantum machine learning (QML) can improve financial crime detection. This initiative will bring together financial institutions, quantum tech providers, and research labs to benchmark quantum algorithms against classical methods using a synthetic dataset, addressing data governance concerns. The QEG also aims to inform regulatory oversight for quantum technologies. The move also underlines the K‑Moonshot strategy’s ambition to translate quantum breakthroughs into commercial value for SMEs, though the true impact will depend on software ecosystems and latency between the two platforms.

South Korea has launched its sixth national supercomputer, Hangang, with a peak performance of 614 petaflops. It is designed to be the high-performance computing backbone for the country's first hybrid quantum-classical computing platform, integrating with IonQ's Tempo quantum processor by May 2027. Hangang will support general research, national strategic R&D, and small to medium enterprises, playing a key role in South Korea's K-Moonshot initiative. item.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a key bottleneck for scalable semiconductor quantum computers by quantifying how the path taken during electron‑spin shuttling directly shapes decoherence and leakage in multi‑spin logical qubits. By deriving compact fidelity formulas that depend only on experimentally accessible pairwise dephasing rates, the authors give hardware teams concrete criteria for choosing parallel versus sequential transport regimes—a distinction that aligns with recent demonstrations of long‑range spin conveyance and emerging fault‑tolerant architectures. The work therefore bridges theory and practice, offering a roadmap to minimize noise‑induced errors as qubit shuttling becomes a central element of future quantum processors.

Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated $1/f$ noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

item.title: Arrival-time problem in the quantum information era - observation of a Zeno crossover in monitored arrival-time distributions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the classic “when does a quantum particle arrive?” question by demonstrating that monitored transport on superconducting processors exhibits a clear crossover between a quantum‑Zeno regime and a low‑monitoring regime, with an optimal measurement cadence set by the particle’s bandwidth. By confirming the theory across single‑particle, interacting many‑body, and two‑dimensional circuits, the work shows that Zeno‑type control is a generic tool for shaping dynamical information flow in quantum hardware—a capability that could be leveraged for error mitigation, state preparation, or quantum sensing protocols. The results also provide the first experimental arrival‑time distributions in a monitored setting, establishing a new benchmark for quantum‑trajectory modeling on near‑term devices.

When does a quantum particle arrive at a detector? The temporal distributions of itinerant quantum particles have been debated since the birth of quantum mechanics. Here we study the arrival-time problem in periodically monitored spin chains and quantum circuits. The arrival dynamics exhibits two regimes, the quantum Zeno and the low-monitoring regime, separated by an optimal monitoring period set by the single-particle bandwidth. In support of the theory, on superconducting quantum hardware, we measure arrival-time distributions for single and multiple interacting particles in one- and two-dimensional circuits. The measured distributions resolve both regimes and agree closely with quantum-trajectory theory. The crossover persists in interacting many-particle systems: the optimal monitoring point is preserved while many-body interference reshapes the distributions. Zeno suppression likewise persists in two-dimensional geometry. Together, these results show that the two regimes are a generic feature of monitored propagation rather than a single-particle effect. To our knowledge, our work constitutes the first experimental measurement of arrival-time distributions in a monitored quantum transport setting, addressing one of the longest-standing problems in quantum mechanics.

item.title: Differentiable Digital Twins for Optimization, Calibration, and Characterization of Neutral-Atom- and Ion-based Quantum Computers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first open‑source “digital twin” that can be differentiated end‑to‑end, letting researchers automatically compute gradients of gate performance for neutral‑atom and trapped‑ion processors. By marrying high‑fidelity physical modeling with quantum optimal control and automatic differentiation, the toolset bridges a gap between hardware characterization and software optimization that has limited fidelity gains in recent experiments on Rydberg arrays and ion chains. The ability to rapidly calibrate and improve gates could accelerate scaling efforts, though its impact will depend on how easily experimental groups can integrate the framework with their existing control stacks.

Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.

item.title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the long‑standing data‑loading bottleneck by presenting deterministic, low‑depth amplitude‑encoding circuits that scale to arbitrarily large vectors without requiring amplitude amplification or mid‑circuit measurement. By recasting multi‑controlled rotations as a Boolean minimisation problem and exploiting an ancilla‑based Walsh–Hadamard decomposition, the authors achieve order‑of‑magnitude reductions in two‑qubit gate count compared with Qiskit’s default state‑preparation routine—a gain they validate on IQM’s square‑lattice hardware. The result opens a practical pathway for near‑term quantum‑machine‑learning and variational algorithms that depend on fast, high‑fidelity state preparation, though the reported depth advantages assume relatively flexible connectivity and may diminish on more constrained devices.

Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.

item.title: Shaping Frequency-Bin Biphoton Correlations via Programmable Optical Frequency Combs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a model‑free, hardware‑in‑the‑loop optimizer can shape the joint spectral intensity of photon pairs generated by a programmable optical frequency comb, tuning up to 22 pump, signal and idler parameters with only two hardware evaluations per iteration. By achieving high Pearson correlations on 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 frequency‑bin grids, it provides a practical route to reconfigurable, high‑dimensional frequency‑bin states that are essential for quantum communication, networking and sensing applications. The work builds on recent efforts to harness broadband nonlinear sources for scalable photonic qudits, but it currently controls only intensity—not spectral phase—so full two‑photon state engineering will still require phase‑sensitive characterization. Nonetheless, the demonstrated fast, parameter‑efficient shaping marks a significant step toward flexible quantum‑optical hardware that can be programmed on demand.

Programmable shaping of photon-pair spectral correlations is important for frequency-bin quantum information processing. However, achieving this control remains challenging in nonlinear optical systems without reliable forward models. Here, we demonstrate model-free, hardware-in-the-loop shaping of the measured joint spectral intensity of a cascaded photon-pair source driven by a programmable optical frequency comb. A blockwise simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation controller optimizes up to 22 pump, signal, and idler parameters. Each iteration requires only two accepted hardware evaluations, independent of the parameter count. The controller converges to diverse target patterns on 3$\times$3, 4$\times$4, and 5$\times$5 frequency-bin grids. The optimized distributions achieve Pearson correlations between 0.66 and 0.98 and classical overlap fidelities between 0.32 and 0.62. Cross-target similarity analysis confirms that the optimized patterns remain target-specific. Source characterization yields a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio of approximately 585. Accuracy is limited by pump-phase transfer, parasitic nonlinear background, waveshaper constraints, amplitude-only filtering, and measurement noise. Joint spectral intensity contains no spectral-phase information. Therefore, the results demonstrate control of measured frequency-bin populations and correlations, not complete reconstruction of the two-photon state. Phase-sensitive characterization is required to verify inter-bin coherence and quantify the entanglement dimensionality of the output state. Our results establish direct measurement feedback as a practical approach to reconfigurable frequency-bin correlation engineering when an accurate end-to-end model is unavailable.

item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Quantum subsets discrimination and key sifting with success probability one
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing limitation of quantum cryptography by showing that error‑free discrimination between subsets of non‑orthogonal, even linearly dependent, states can be achieved with unit success probability—a feat previously thought impossible without sacrificing determinism. By turning the subset‑discrimination protocol into an alternative basis‑reconciliation step, it promises sifting efficiencies of 100 % for multi‑basis or high‑dimensional QKD schemes, potentially closing the gap between theoretical key rates and practical implementations. The result builds on recent advances in probabilistic orthogonalization and could reshape how future quantum‑secure networks handle state preparation and measurement, though experimental realization will hinge on implementing the required collective measurements with low overhead.

Non-distinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states is the essential feature of quantum mechanics. In particular, one cannot deterministically orthogonalize the set of quantum states, while probabilistic orthogonalization is possible, including unambiguous state discrimination and discrimination between the subsets. Here, we propose a method for error-free subsets discrimination with significantly increased success probability, which may reach one even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent input states. This method may be applied in quantum cryptography: An alternative basis reconciliation procedure is described, which may provide unit sifting probability even for a large number of bases and for non-orthogonal states within each basis.

item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Magic Can Superactivate Quantum Capacity
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that “magic”—the non‑stabilizer resource essential for universal quantum computation—can act as a catalyst that turns two otherwise useless channels into a conduit for genuine quantum information, extending the classic superactivation phenomenon to a new class of Clifford‑based convolutional channels. By linking magic to channel capacity through a concrete construction with mixed‑magic environments and half‑erasure auxiliaries, the work bridges abstract resource theories and practical communication models, suggesting that engineered noisy environments could be harnessed rather than merely mitigated. The result sharpens our understanding of what physical resources are truly required for quantum transmission and sets a benchmark for future protocols that aim to exploit non‑stabilizer noise as an asset rather than a liability.

Environmental magic can enable two channels with zero quantum capacity to transmit quantum information jointly. We establish this superactivation within a family of discrete quantum convolution channels with fixed Clifford interactions. For the couplings considered, stabilizer-mixture environments induce entanglement-breaking channels. We construct a mixed magic environment whose induced channel has positive private capacity and a Choi state with positive partial transpose, hence zero quantum capacity. A half-erasure auxiliary activates this channel through the Smith--Yard mechanism. Finite-block encoding and decoding over a self-complementary convolution auxiliary then realize a higher-dimensional erasure channel that still permits activation. We also bound the activated capacity by the modified relative entropy of magic of the main environment. Replacing either environment of the convolution pair by any stabilizer mixture makes the joint quantum capacity vanish, identifying environmental magic as a necessary resource on both sides for this realization.

item.title: Study Maps 24 Problems Where Quantum Computers Could Gain an Edge
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it provides the first systematic inventory of twenty‑four concrete problems where quantum computers could realistically outperform classical methods, giving the field a clearer roadmap for algorithm development and hardware targets. item.title: Quantum Interference Control of Coupled Atomic Spins
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that Landau‑Zener‑Stückelberg‑Majorana interference can be harnessed for fully electrical, non‑resonant manipulation of individual atomic spins, turning a Ti‑Ti‑Fe trimer on MgO into a fast, low‑decoherence qubit platform. By engineering avoided crossings with combined magnetic fields and bias voltage, the authors achieve remote spin control via the Fe atom’s stray field, sidestepping the disruptive tunneling currents that have limited previous ESR‑STM approaches. The work provides a concrete pathway toward scalable atom‑based quantum processors by showing how quantum interference can replace microwave driving for rapid, coherent gate operations.

We propose a protocol for the non-resonant electric control of quantum states in atomic-scale spin systems using Landau-Zener-Stückelberg-Majorana (LZSM) interferometry. We focus on a Ti-Ti-Fe trimer on a thin MgO layer, a platform that has recently emerged as a promising candidate for qubit realization using electron spin resonance combined with scanning tunneling microscopy (ESR-STM). We first analyze a Ti dimer in the absence of the Fe atom and show, through a detailed spectroscopic study, that avoided level crossings can be engineered by combining the in-plane component of the external magnetic field, the tip magnetic field, and the applied bias voltage, which allows the system to be tuned electrically through these crossings. Based on this, we develop LZSM protocols for coherent state control in the dimer using non-resonant LZSM-STM. We then consider the full trimer, where the Fe atom generates a local magnetic field at the remote Ti atom, enabling non-local spin control. We show that this remote and non-resonant manipulation reduces unwanted effects associated with tunneling electrons and enables quantum operations on short timescales. Our results show that quantum interference can be used as a resource for electrically driven, non-resonant, and non-local spin control in atomic-scale systems. This approach enables fast quantum operations while mitigating decoherence, offering a promising route toward scalable atom-based qubit architectures.

item.title: Twisted Compactification, Quotient Quantum Codes and Logical Gates
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reveals that a broad class of quantum error‑correcting codes can be understood as “twisted compactifications,” turning the abstract notion of quotient codes into a concrete geometric construction that directly yields logical qudits, operators and distance bounds from a parent stabilizer code. By exploiting Tate cohomology and higher‑form symmetries, the authors generate non‑Pauli stabilizer codes with linear distance and demonstrate how specific twists produce native multi‑qubit gates such as CCZ, addressing a long‑standing goal of achieving fault‑tolerant non‑Clifford operations without magic‑state overhead. The framework unifies recent developments in product‑code families, topological order beyond abelian anyons, and transversal gate design, offering a systematic toolkit for building more powerful, scalable quantum memories.

Many quantum codes, including balanced-product, bivariate-bicycle and genon codes and the five-qubit code, are quotient codes: a larger code folded onto itself by identifying each check with its image under a deck transformation composed with a symmetry. We show that this is the lattice form of twisted compactification, in which a theory on $X\times F$ carries a symmetry background along $F$, and we use the correspondence in both directions. For monomial quotients of Pauli stabilizer codes, a transfer theorem gives the logical qudits, logical operators and distance bounds from those of the parent, with a Tate cohomology group counting the logical operators that are new. For higher-form and cup-product symmetries the twist is an entangling diagonal circuit; when a finite cover trivializes the background, the code is a dressed quotient, so abelian Pauli codes give non-abelian topological order such as $D(D_4)$. The dressings have Clifford level at most one less than the degree of the twist, and for cubic twists the code dimension is a count of solutions of quadratic equations in cup products, which certifies that the code is not a Pauli stabilizer code when it is not a power of two; on tori and slabs the distance is linear in the size. Twists also create logical gates: three toric codes on $S^3$ have no logical qubits, but on $\mathbb{RP}^3$ the same circuit is a logical $CCZ$. A quarter-turn twist of the 3D fermionic toric code gives codes of linear distance, from $[[768,2,9]]$ up, whose $p+ip$ pump is an explicit finite-time quasi-local evolution that preserves the code space exactly; using the spin-topological response formula of Barkeshli, Hsin and Kobayashi, we identify its logical action as $T$ up to Clifford factors. Finally, twisting abelian gauge theories reach only the quantum doubles $D(G)$ with $[G,G]$ central.

item.title: Direct-decision quantum sensing for classifying transient NMR signals
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates how a task‑oriented quantum sensor can bypass full signal reconstruction and output a binary decision directly, offering a clear advantage over conventional coil readout when the inductive link is weak or noisy. By interleaving trainable control pulses with the qubit’s evolution, the authors show that ensemble‑averaged accuracy can rise sharply for certain NMR‑like waveforms—mirroring recent progress in variational quantum classifiers applied to sensing problems. The work also highlights practical limits: single‑shot discrimination remains gradual and requires either long interrogation times or unusually strong sensor coupling, underscoring the need for improved qubit–sample interfaces before such protocols become a routine tool for small‑volume molecular detection.

Task-oriented quantum sensing aims to extract decision-relevant information directly, without first reconstructing the full signal. We study this approach for mixture-threshold classification of transient NMR-like signals generated from molecular spin Hamiltonians, motivated by small-volume molecular sensing. Using analytical models and numerical simulations, we compare classical coil readout followed by matched-filter classification with quantum computational sensing (QCS), in which trainable controls interleaved with signal-driven sensor-qubit evolution map the transient directly to a decision score. We consider both the sensor-ensemble limit and strict single-sensor single-shot readout. Increasing QCS control depth can improve robustness and class-dependent output contrast. Ensemble accuracy can rise rapidly for some waveform pairs, whereas single-shot correctness improves more gradually because one projective outcome must distinguish the classes. Repeated acquisitions improve both routes by averaging independent fluctuations, while disorder-aware training mitigates quasistatic inhomogeneity in the modeled sensor ensemble. QCS can outperform inductive readout under the modeled conditions, for example when coil transfer is weak or receiver noise limits coil performance. However, the simulated QCS protocols at lower effective sensor coupling require long sensing intervals, whereas short-time protocols require a much stronger effective drive at the sensor. Practical advantage therefore depends on jointly attainable source-signal strength, signal-to-sensor transfer, qubit coherence, and readout resources.

item.title: Sharp error tolerance of the monogamy-of-entanglement game
item.description:

By proving exponential decay under parallel repetition even when players use non‑identical answer strings, the work strengthens security reductions for quantum key distribution, position verification and unclonable encryption. The result dovetails with recent advances in device‑independent cryptography that seek tighter composability guarantees, making it a timely boost to both theory and real‑world implementations.

The BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement (MoE) game has numerous applications in quantum cryptography, including quantum key distribution, position verification, and unclonable encryption. In this short note, we improve the error threshold for parallel repetition with identical answer strings from the approximately $3.7\%$ certified by the original bound to the sharp threshold $(1-1/\sqrt2)/2\approx14.64\%$. When the players need not give identical answers, we also obtain exponential decay whenever the sum of their error tolerances is below this threshold. These bounds strengthen existing security reductions to the BB84 MoE game, improving security bounds and certified noise tolerances for cryptographic protocols.

item.title: Optimal performance of driven-dissipative many-body quantum batteries beyond complete nonreciprocity
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article overturns the prevailing belief that complete nonreciprocity is the universal sweet spot for driven‑dissipative quantum batteries, showing instead that the optimal charging performance emerges from a nuanced balance of coherent couplings and both local and collective dissipation rates. By identifying the Dzyaloshinskii‑Moriya interaction as the most effective link in weakly driven two‑qubit setups—and demonstrating how engineered shared reservoirs can boost extractable work even when they lower raw capacity—the work provides concrete design rules for scalable many‑body battery architectures. The findings bridge a gap between theoretical proposals and hardware implementation, suggesting that future quantum processors could harvest energy more efficiently by tailoring dissipation pathways rather than relying on idealized nonreciprocal conditions.

Proposals for nonreciprocal quantum batteries identify the point of complete nonreciprocity, where coherent and reservoir-mediated couplings balance, as the operating point for enhanced charging. We show that, for batteries built from interacting qubits, this point is, in general, suboptimal. The optimal design is set by a more intricate interplay between the coherent coupling and the local and collective dissipation rates, of which complete nonreciprocity is only a special case. We consider a many-body battery charged by a driven many-body charger, with each qubit coupled to a local bath and the complete setup immersed in a shared engineered reservoir. For a weakly driven two-qubit setup, we prove the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction to be the optimal coupling, and show that the battery capacity is maximized at a coupling strength fixed by the local and collective dissipation rates, which coincides with complete nonreciprocity only for a specific balance between them. The shared reservoir enhances the capacity for couplings weaker or stronger than both local dissipation rates, and can increase the extractable work even where it reduces the capacity. At strong drive, with the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction between the charger and the battery, the capacity is bounded by $1/2$. For qubits arranged in a star network with a single central battery qubit, these results remain qualitatively unchanged, while the maximum capacity of a battery charged by $N_A$ weakly driven charger qubits saturates with $N_A$ in the presence of the shared reservoir, approaching its limit as $N_A^{-1}$. In contrast, the maximum capacity of $N_B$ qubit batteries charged by a single-qubit charger decays as $N_B^{-2}$.

item.title: Critical properties of EPR steering
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that even the weakest‑entangled two‑qubit states can be turned into a genuine EPR‑steering resource simply by measuring two copies together, revealing a sharp “critical” point where the required measurement entanglement drops to zero. By disentangling the roles of measurement entanglement, number of settings and collective access, the work clarifies why some states appear unsteerable in single‑shot experiments yet become useful for quantum‑enhanced sensing or semi‑device‑independent protocols when modest resources are pooled. The construction of high‑dimensional states that gain steering on two copies while remaining Bell‑local over many copies also settles the long‑standing amplification question, suggesting new pathways to certify entanglement in noisy hardware without demanding full Bell violations.

Every PVM-critical entangled two-qubit state becomes steerable with two copies. We prove this for the full critical boundary and for two different critical inputs. The joint measurements can have arbitrarily little entanglement, while all conditional states on Bob's two systems remain separable. Criticality is exactly the point where this measurement-entanglement threshold vanishes. The number of measurements has a separate critical behavior: every fixed setting bound leaves an unsteerable neighborhood of the critical input. Moreover, for any such bound, there are critical states that remain unsteerable under every tensor power, although unrestricted measurements activate them with two copies. These results identify different roles for measurement entanglement, measurement number, and collective access in revealing steering. We also construct fixed-dimensional states whose steering activates on two copies while Bell locality persists through any prescribed finite copy range. In increasing dimension, the two-copy steering violation is unbounded, giving an affirmative solution to the amplification question of Hsieh, Liang, and Lee.

item.title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is timely because it bridges the gap between rapidly maturing DV‑QKD hardware and the often‑overlooked software stack that actually delivers secure keys, offering a hands‑on guide to the most efficient reconciliation codes—from Cascade to polar codes—within an easy‑to‑use GUI framework. By benchmarking asymptotic versus finite‑size secret‑key rates against real‑world post‑processing performance, it gives system designers concrete data on how close practical implementations can approach theoretical limits. The open server‑client architecture also lowers the barrier for labs and startups to prototype end‑to‑end QKD links without writing low‑level code from scratch. Readers should note that while the tutorial streamlines algorithm selection, achieving optimal SKR still depends on careful tuning of channel parameters such as QBER and block size.

Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.

By juxtaposing teacher–student configurations with the specific quantum resources used—ranging from raw measurement probabilities to full‑circuit objectives—it clarifies where genuine quantum advantage has been demonstrated versus where results remain marginal or hardware‑limited. The survey’s critical assessment of experimental evidence and its call for standardized reporting give researchers a concrete roadmap for turning these promising ideas into reproducible, scalable applications.

Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

item.title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that boron‑nitride nanotubes can host bright, room‑temperature single‑photon emitters across the visible spectrum with lifetimes as short as 0.5 ns—roughly twice as fast as the best hBN flakes reported to date. By packing multiple spectrally distinct emitters along a ~25 nm‑diameter tube and demonstrating that surface coating suppresses blinking, the work offers a compact, multi‑wavelength source that can be positioned deterministically in photonic circuits, addressing a long‑standing bottleneck for scalable quantum key distribution hardware. The results complement recent advances in 2D hBN emitters while sidestepping their integration challenges, though further work will be needed to verify long‑term stability and coupling efficiency in realistic device architectures.

Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

item.title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the number of physical Pauli recovery gates needed for repetition‑code process tomography can be dramatically reduced—down to zero for three qubits and just five for seven—by exhaustively searching optimal decoder designs rather than relying on the conventional minimum‑weight rule. The resulting gate‑optimal decoders deliver up to an order‑of‑magnitude improvement in tomographic precision while cutting experimental runtime, a benefit that directly supports current efforts to benchmark and calibrate noisy intermediate‑scale quantum processors more efficiently. However, the advantage diminishes for larger codes where full decoding can even lose rank, underscoring that scaling these techniques will require careful conditioning of hardware and possibly new decoder heuristics.

Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at $n=3$ is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.5$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them ($1.8$ to $88$ times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a $10$\,mrad rms error then costs $1.2\times10^{7}$ shots in $65$\,s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while $n\ge5$ stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.

item.title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes the quantum‑internet vision beyond merely ferrying qubits, arguing that core network functions themselves can be built on quantum phenomena such as entanglement superposition and non‑local connectivity. By treating entanglement as a stateful, visible resource, it opens a design space for truly “quantum‑native” routing, addressing and topology that could cut overhead and enable new distributed algorithms. The proposal dovetails with recent efforts to embed entanglement‑based primitives into networking stacks, signaling a shift toward infrastructure where the network’s logic is intrinsically quantum. Practical impact will hinge on overcoming decoherence and demonstrating these concepts on real hardware.

The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.
